blocks.text: Given three integers a, b, and c, find the minimum number of bits that need to be flipped in a and b (combined) so that the bitwise OR of a and b equals c.

blocks.title: Analogy: Adjusting Two Dimmer Switches to Match a Target Reading
blocks.text: Like having two rows of on-off switches whose combined "any switch on" reading needs to match a target pattern exactly, and counting the fewest individual switch flips across both rows needed to make that happen.

blocks.caption: Flip the fewest bits across a and b so that their bitwise OR matches c exactly

blocks.text: Here a OR b is already 1 OR 2 equals 3, exactly matching c, so 0 flips are needed at all.

Before writing any bitwise expressions, notice that every bit position's flip requirement depends only on 3 independent boolean facts at that position: a's bit, b's bit, and c's bit, with no interaction between different positions at all.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since a, b, and c's bit at any position are each independently 0 or 1, there are only 8 possible combinations at any bit position, and only a small handful of them ever require a flip.

Observation 2: If c's bit is 0, every 1 bit present in a or b at that position must individually be flipped off, contributing 1 flip each, so up to 2 flips can be needed at a single position.

Observation 3: If c's bit is 1, at most 1 flip is ever needed, and only when neither a nor b already has a 1 there; if either one already does, the OR already satisfies c and no flip is needed.

Observation 4: Each of these three flip-contributing conditions, "a has an extra 1 where c wants 0", "b has an extra 1 where c wants 0", and "c wants a 1 but neither a nor b provides one", is itself expressible as a bitwise AND of the right operands, possibly negated, so counting how many bit positions satisfy each condition is just a population count of that AND expression.

Whenever a per-bit decision only depends on a small, fixed number of boolean inputs at that same position, write the decision as a bitwise expression and take its popcount, replacing a 32-iteration branching loop with a small, fixed number of whole-integer operations.

This turns 3 separate per-position branches into 3 direct popcount expressions evaluated once each over the entire integer, a pattern useful whenever bit positions are truly independent of one another.

Check every one of the 32 bit positions individually, extracting the corresponding bit from a, b, and c, and use explicit conditional branches to determine and add up how many flips are needed at that position.

items: For each bit position, extract the bit of a, b, and c there.
If c's bit is 0, count how many of a and b have a 1 there, since each one needs to be flipped off.
If c's bit is 1 but both a and b have 0 there, exactly one flip is needed to turn either one on.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: All three relevant bits, bit_a, bit_b, and bit_c, are extracted up front at each position, since the branching logic that follows needs to inspect all three together, not just one at a time.

The two cases are structured as bit_c == 0 versus bit_c == 1, since a position where c wants a 0 can need up to 2 flips (both a and b), while a position where c wants a 1 can need at most 1 flip, a fundamentally different flip count ceiling per case.

total += bit_a + bit_b directly adds 0, 1, or 2 depending on how many of a and b are set, rather than writing two separate if-statements for a and b individually, since simply summing the two 0/1 bit values already produces the correct flip count for that branch.

blocks.text: Every bit position's exact flip requirement is directly computed and summed, so the true minimum flip count is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), a fixed number of position checks.
Space: O(1), only a running total is kept.

Limitation: although already fast, this relies on explicit per-position branching logic with several cases to get right, when the whole computation can instead be expressed directly as a small number of bitwise expressions with no branching at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force is already O(32), effectively constant time, so there is no asymptotic bottleneck left to remove; what remains is the branching itself, several nested conditionals repeated 32 times that must all be gotten exactly right. Looking closely at those conditionals, each one is really just testing a fixed combination of a's bit, b's bit, and c's bit, existence questions that bitwise AND and NOT can express directly without ever touching an explicit bit index. "A bit of a is set where c is not" is exactly a AND (NOT c). "A bit of b is set where c is not" is exactly b AND (NOT c). "Neither a nor b is set where c is" is exactly c AND (NOT a) AND (NOT b). Once each condition is written as a single whole-integer expression, counting how many bit positions satisfy it is just a population count, collapsing the entire 32-iteration branching loop into 3 popcount calls.

The total flip count can be expressed directly as a sum of three population counts computed over whole numbers at once, with no per-bit branching: the count of set bits in a that are at a position where c is 0 (each needs turning off), plus the count of set bits in b at a position where c is 0 (each also needs turning off), plus the count of positions where c is 1 but neither a nor b has a bit set there (each needs exactly one flip to turn on).
Compute the answer directly as popcount(a AND NOT c) plus popcount(b AND NOT c) plus popcount(c AND NOT a AND NOT b).

blocks.caption: Optimized: three whole-number bitwise expressions, each with a direct popcount, no per-bit branching

codes.python:
def min_flips(a, b, c):
    not_c = ~c
    turn_off_a = bin(a & not_c).count('1')                    # bits of a that must be turned off
    turn_off_b = bin(b & not_c).count('1')                      # bits of b that must be turned off
    turn_on = bin(c & ~a & ~b).count('1')                        # bits where neither a nor b has a 1, but c needs one
    return turn_off_a + turn_off_b + turn_on


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(min_flips(2, 6, 5))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) using a hardware popcount instruction, or O(32) with a manual bit counting loop.
Space: O(1), only a few intermediate values are kept.

The three bitwise expressions partition every possible per-bit scenario into exactly the cases that require a flip, with no overlap between them: a bit position contributing to a AND NOT c can never also contribute to c AND NOT a AND NOT b, since the first requires c's bit to be 0 and the second requires it to be 1. Because the three counted sets of positions are mutually exclusive, simply adding their three popcounts gives the exact total flip count, with no double counting and nothing missed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Expression","Positions it counts"],"rows":[["a & ~c","Where a has a 1 bit but c wants a 0 there: a must be flipped off"],["b & ~c","Where b has a 1 bit but c wants a 0 there: b must be flipped off"],["c & ~a & ~b","Where c wants a 1 but neither a nor b has one: either a or b must be flipped on"]]}

items: ~c computes the bitwise NOT of c once, so it can be reused in both the turn_off_a and turn_off_b expressions without recomputing it twice.
a & ~c isolates exactly the bits where a is 1 and c is 0, matching the "must flip a off" condition directly, with no loop needed.
bin(...).count('1') / Integer.bitCount(...) / __builtin_popcount(...) counts the set bits of each expression's result in one call, replacing an explicit per-bit counting loop.
The three popcounts are computed entirely independently of each other and simply summed, since the underlying bit positions they each count never overlap.

blocks.text: This problem rewards recognizing that a per-bit conditional decision (based on 3 boolean values at each position) can often be collapsed into a small number of direct bitwise expressions evaluated over entire integers at once, removing branching entirely in favor of population counts.

items: Miscounting the case where c is 0 but both a and b have a 1 there, forgetting that this requires 2 separate flips, not just 1, since both extra bits must independently be turned off.

Forgetting that the bitwise NOT needs to be interpreted within the relevant bit width in some languages, since NOT on a signed integer type also flips higher order bits that do not matter here but can confuse debugging output if inspected directly.

Assuming the three popcount terms could overlap and need deduplication, when they are actually always mutually exclusive by construction, since each depends on a different, non-overlapping combination of c's bit being 0 or 1.

items: Derive the closed form expression on the whiteboard by walking through the truth table of the 3 possible bit combinations (c is 0, c is 1 with neither set, c is 1 with at least one set) rather than presenting it as a memorized formula, since deriving it demonstrates real understanding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Minimum flips or changes to make a bitwise combination equal a target" points toward per-bit case analysis first to find the flip rule, then expressing that rule as bitwise AND/NOT/OR expressions and taking a popcount, instead of writing an explicit per-bit loop.

items: How would this change if the operation were AND instead of OR? The per-bit truth table changes completely: a target 1 requires both a and b to be 1, so any missing one needs exactly one flip, while a target 0 only requires at least one of them to become 0, changing which bitwise expressions apply.

What if only a could be modified, not b? The problem simplifies to directly comparing a against a target derived from b and c, effectively reducing to counting differing bits between a and that derived target.

Can this be generalized to more than two source numbers ORed together? Yes, the same style of per-bit case analysis still applies, though the truth table over more source bits grows larger and the resulting bitwise expressions become more involved.
Same "derive a per-bit truth table, then express it as a bitwise expression plus popcount" technique as Total Hamming Distance's per-bit-position counting.
Same branchless bit-counting philosophy as UTF-8 Validation's leading-1-bit count, replacing explicit conditionals with a direct arithmetic or bitwise computation.
Same "partition into mutually exclusive counted cases, then sum" reasoning used broadly whenever a total count is built from several non-overlapping bitwise conditions.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(32) time with per-bit branching, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(1) time with hardware popcount (or O(32) with a manual count), O(1) space, using 3 direct bitwise expressions instead of branching.

items: Pattern: Per-bit truth-table case analysis collapsed into bitwise AND/NOT expressions plus popcount

Core Idea: Every bit position's flip requirement depends only on that position's own bits of a, b, and c, so the total is a sum of three mutually exclusive popcounts, each expressible as a single bitwise expression
Time: O(1) with hardware popcount, O(32) with a manual bit count
Space: O(1)

Most Important Observation: A per-bit conditional decision that depends on a small fixed number of boolean inputs can always be rewritten as a bitwise expression and counted with popcount, removing branching entirely
Interview Difficulty: Medium to Hard
One-line memory trick: Three non-overlapping popcounts: turn a off, turn b off, turn either on
